html:
The 2003 Bam earthquake struck the city of Bam in Kerman province, southeastern Iran, early in the morning of 26 December 2003. With a magnitude of about 6.6, it killed at least 26,000 people and destroyed most of the city.

Bam was an oasis town famous for its dates and for the Arg-e Bam, a vast citadel and walled town built of mud brick, sun-dried clay and straw. The citadel had stood for many centuries, perhaps since the Achaemenid era or soon after, and much of what stood was rebuilt in the Safavid period.

The quake was centred right under the city and was shallow. Mud-brick houses collapsed into heavy rubble that left little air for survivors, and many people were asleep. The citadel was largely destroyed.

Aid came from around the world, including, briefly, from the United States, though relations with the revolutionary government were hostile. In 2004 UNESCO listed Bam and its cultural landscape as a World Heritage Site in danger, and restoration of the citadel has gone on since. Compare the 1960 Agadir earthquake.
